questions.prompt: A CI job runs `claude -p "write the release notes"` and produces a different answer on the runner than on the developer's laptop. The repository is identical on both. What is the most likely cause, and the fix?
options: The model is non-deterministic, so install a fixed seed with a flag
The run loads the host's context (CLAUDE.md, hooks, skills, MCP); re-run with no dependency on it by using `--bare` and passing only what the job needs
The runner is slower, so add `--max-turns` to force the same path
The prompt is too vague; make it more specific so any machine agrees
questions.explanation: A `-p` run uses the same context loader as an interactive session: it reads the working directory's and the home directory's .claude, CLAUDE.md, hooks, skills, MCP servers, and auto memory. On the laptop that set is rich; on a clean runner it is empty, so the same command has different inputs. `--bare` skips auto-discovery and makes the run depend only on what the script passes, which is what reproducibility requires. A is the tempting answer because model sampling is real, but the sample space cannot explain a difference that tracks the machine, and no seed flag fixes configuration drift. C confuses speed with context. D assumes the prompt is where the difference lives, but the prompt was the same on both machines.

questions.prompt: A nightly `claude -p` job sometimes runs for an hour and then times out instead of finishing. The task itself is quick. What should you change first?
options: Raise the job timeout so it has room to finish
Add `--permission-prompts none` (and/or an explicit `--allowedTools` list) so a tool call can't sit waiting for an approval
Switch `--output-format` to `stream-json` so the job streams instead of blocking
Run it with `--continue` so it resumes past the stall
questions.explanation: A `-p` run still follows the permission system. When a tool call needs approval and no human is present, the run waits — which is exactly a quick task that occasionally takes an hour. `--permission-prompts none` tells the run nobody can answer: anything that would prompt is denied, Claude is told not to retry, and the run proceeds. `--allowedTools` pre-approves the tools that legitimately need to run. A is tempting because a timeout is the visible symptom, but a larger timeout just changes how long the hang lasts. C changes how output is delivered, not whether approval is needed. D continues a finished conversation; there is nothing to resume when the run never ended.

questions.prompt: A script must pull an array of function names out of a file's contents. Which approach is the robust one?
options: Run with default text output and extract the names with a regular expression
Run with `--output-format json --json-schema '{...}'` and read the validated `structured_output` field
Ask the model to format the names as a comma-separated string and split on commas
Turn the prompt into several `-p` calls, one per function, and concatenate
questions.explanation: A JSON Schema turns the answer into a validated contract: the response carries a `structured_output` field shaped the way you asked, so your script parses a field instead of guessing at prose. A is tempting because it is what you do with an ordinary command, but scraping free text couples your script to the model's formatting, which changes without warning. C replaces a schema with a delimiter convention that the model may not honor, and names containing commas break it outright. D multiplies cost and calls without removing the parsing problem, since each call still returns prose.
